If something or someone is unreliable, it means you cannot depend on them to do what they are supposed to do, or to behave the way you expect them to.

Think of it this way: when you rely on something, you count on it. You trust it will work. When something is *un*reliable, that trust is broken — not necessarily once, but as a pattern. You can't count on it.
The Heart of the Word

The most important idea inside "unreliable" is inconsistency + inability to be counted on.

Something unreliable:

  • Does not consistently perform as expected
  • Cannot be trusted to show up, work, or do what is needed
  • Makes planning around it risky or difficult
  • Creates doubt in your mind every time you need it
People Can Be Unreliable

When a person is unreliable, they regularly fail to do what they promised or were expected to do. They might:

  • Cancel plans at the last moment
  • Miss deadlines frequently
  • Say they will do something but not follow through
  • Behave unpredictably — you never know what to expect from them

Example: "Don't assign that project to him — he's unreliable and always misses his deadlines."

An important point: an unreliable person is not necessarily dishonest or bad-intentioned. They might genuinely mean to do what they say. The problem is they simply cannot be counted on to actually do it. A person can have good intentions but still be unreliable. This is what separates "unreliable" from "dishonest" — dishonesty is about lying; unreliability is about failing to deliver.
Objects and Systems Can Be Unreliable

A machine, tool, or service is unreliable when it does not work consistently — it functions sometimes, but fails at unpredictable moments.

Examples:

  • "My old car is unreliable — it breaks down at least once a month."
  • "The Wi-Fi in that building is unreliable; it cuts out several times a day."
  • "The electricity supply in that village is unreliable — the power goes out without warning."

The key idea is not that it never works, but that you can never be sure it will work when you need it to.
Information Can Be Unreliable

This is a very important and common use of the word. When information, data, a source, or a memory is unreliable, it means you cannot fully trust it to be accurate or true.

Examples:

  • "That website is unreliable — it often publishes false information."
  • "His memory is unreliable; he remembers events differently every time he tells the story."
  • "The test results were unreliable because the equipment was faulty."

In literature, an unreliable narrator is a character who tells the story, but whose account cannot be fully trusted — they may be lying, mistaken, deluded, or biased, so the reader cannot take everything they say at face value.
Degrees: How Unreliable Can Something Be?

Unreliability exists on a scale. Something can be:

  • Slightly unreliable — it fails occasionally, but usually works fine. (A train that is sometimes 10 minutes late.)
  • Fairly unreliable — it fails often enough that you start planning around the possibility of failure. (A printer that jams every few days.)
  • Completely unreliable — it fails so often that you essentially cannot depend on it at all. (A car that won't start more days than it does.)

You'll often see it strengthened with words like: notoriously unreliable, highly unreliable, completely unreliable, deeply unreliable.
What "Unreliable" Does NOT Mean

This is worth being clear about, because learners often mix these up:

  • Unreliable ≠ Incompetent. A person can be very skilled but still unreliable. A brilliant surgeon who always cancels appointments is unreliable — it's not about their skill, it's about their consistency.
  • Unreliable ≠ Dishonest. As noted above, an unreliable person can be completely honest. The problem is follow-through, not truthfulness.
  • Unreliable ≠ Bad. It is a negative quality, but it's specific. You'd use "bad" for many reasons; "unreliable" is for one specific flaw — the inability to be counted on.
The Tone and Feeling of the Word

"Unreliable" carries a negative connotation — it implies disappointment, broken trust, or frustration. When someone calls a person unreliable, it's a serious criticism in professional or personal contexts. It suggests a pattern of letting people down.

However, when used for objects or information, the tone is more neutral and descriptive — it simply signals caution. "Use a more reliable source" is advice, not an insult.
Related Word Forms You Should Know

FormExample
  • Unreliably (adverb) — describes how something behaves. "The machine works unreliably."
  • Unreliability (noun) — the quality or state of being unreliable. "His unreliability cost him the job."
  • Reliable (opposite adjective) — dependable, consistent, trustworthy. "She is a reliable employee."
  • Reliability (opposite noun) — the quality of being reliable. "The reliability of this car is excellent."
Synonyms — and How They Differ

Understanding similar words helps you understand the precise meaning of "unreliable":

  • Undependable — almost identical in meaning; the most direct synonym. Interchangeable with "unreliable" in most contexts.
  • Inconsistent — focuses specifically on the variation in behavior. An inconsistent person does something well sometimes and poorly other times; "unreliable" focuses more on not being able to count on them at all.
  • Untrustworthy — stronger and more personal; implies the possibility of deception or bad intentions. More damaging than "unreliable."
  • Erratic — unpredictable and irregular in behavior, with no clear pattern. An erratic person is wild and unpredictable; an unreliable person may be predictably bad at keeping promises.
  • Flaky (informal/casual) — commonly used in everyday speech, especially for people who cancel plans or don't follow through. "She's so flaky — she bailed on us again." Less formal than "unreliable."
  • Fickle — changes opinions, feelings, or loyalties unpredictably. A fickle person is inconsistent in their feelings. This is a narrower word than "unreliable."
Quick Summary

Unreliable = cannot be depended upon to consistently do what is expected or needed.

It applies to people (who fail to keep promises or show up), to things (that fail to work consistently), and to information (that cannot be trusted to be accurate). It is always a negative quality, but its severity depends on context and degree. The core of the word is this: when something is unreliable, you cannot safely plan around it, because you don't know if it will come through for you.
